# Open DS: every scheme in full

> Generated from schemes/*.json. Each scheme lists its answers (question: answer. why), its usage rules (situation: use; not; why) and its voice.

## Color guidance, for every scheme

Status colors go up in urgency: info, then warning, then danger. Pick the level that matches the real risk. Never go up a level to get attention. Success sits outside the order.
Urgency order: color.status.info.@ → color.status.warning.@ → color.status.danger.@

- color.surface.canvas: The page background behind everything. Use for: Page and app background. Not for: Cards and panels on the page (use color.surface.default).
- color.surface.default: The base fill for content. Use for: Cards, Panels, Inputs, Table body. Not for: The page behind content (use color.surface.canvas); Menus and popovers above content (use color.surface.raised).
- color.surface.raised: Fills that float above content. In dark, one step lighter than content, so height reads by tone. Use for: Menus, Popovers, Dialogs. Not for: Cards in the page flow (use color.surface.default).
- color.surface.sunken: A recessed fill, a step below content. Use for: Table headers, Wells. Not for: A selected item (use color.surface.selected); An item the pointer or the keyboard is on (use color.surface.highlight).
- color.surface.highlight: The fill of the item the pointer or the keyboard is on, or whose submenu is open. A state shows on the item's background, one step from the surfaces it sits on: darker in light, and darker in dark too, as raised layers take the lighter step. Use for: Highlighted menu items, Highlighted options, Hover rows, Open submenu triggers. Not for: Table headers and wells (use color.surface.sunken); A selected or current item (use color.surface.selected).
- color.surface.pressed: The fill of an item while it is pressed. Where the scheme gives pressed its own value, one step past the highlight; where pressed reuses hover, the highlight's step. Use for: Pressed menu buttons, Pressed list items. Not for: The item the pointer or the keyboard is on (use color.surface.highlight).
- color.surface.selected: The fill of a selected or current item, or a toggle that is on. Use for: Selected rows, Current menu item, Toggles that are on. Not for: Hover (use color.surface.sunken); The main action (use color.action.primary.@).
- color.surface.inverse: A reversed fill for small, short-lived messages. Use for: Tooltips, Toasts. Not for: Large areas (use color.surface.default).
- color.surface.scrim: The see-through layer behind a modal. Use for: Behind dialogs and sheets. Not for: A solid fill (use color.surface.raised).
- color.text.primary: Body text and headings. Use for: Body text, Headings, Tag labels. Not for: Text on the main action (use color.text.on-action); Text on an inverse fill (use color.text.inverse). Sits on: fills of its tone: color.surface.canvas, color.surface.default, color.surface.raised, color.surface.sunken, color.surface.highlight, color.surface.pressed, color.surface.selected, color.surface.inverse, color.action.primary.@, color.action.primary.hover, color.action.danger.@, color.action.danger.hover, color.action.secondary.@, color.action.secondary.hover, color.status.info.subtle, color.status.warning.subtle, color.status.danger.subtle, color.status.success.subtle at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.text.secondary: Supporting text. Use for: Labels, Descriptions, Metadata. Not for: The main content (use color.text.primary). Sits on: fills of its tone: color.surface.canvas, color.surface.default, color.surface.raised, color.surface.sunken, color.surface.highlight, color.surface.pressed, color.surface.selected at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.text.muted: The quietest text. Use for: Placeholders, Hints, Timestamps. Not for: Anything people must read to act (use color.text.secondary); A disabled control (use color.disabled.text). Sits on: fills of its tone: color.surface.canvas, color.surface.default, color.surface.raised, color.surface.sunken, color.surface.highlight, color.surface.selected at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.text.inverse: Text on an inverse fill. Use for: Tooltip and toast text. Not for: Text on the page (use color.text.primary). Sits on: color.surface.inverse at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.text.on-light: Text on any fill whose tone is light, in either mode: the light mode's body text. Use for: Labels on light fills, The danger and primary buttons in dark mode. Not for: Text on the page's own surfaces (use color.text.primary). Sits on: fills of its tone: color.surface.canvas, color.surface.default, color.surface.raised, color.surface.sunken, color.surface.highlight, color.surface.pressed, color.surface.selected, color.surface.inverse, color.action.primary.@, color.action.primary.hover, color.action.danger.@, color.action.danger.hover, color.action.secondary.@, color.action.secondary.hover, color.status.info.subtle, color.status.warning.subtle, color.status.danger.subtle, color.status.success.subtle at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.text.on-dark: Text on any fill whose tone is dark, in either mode: white. Use for: Labels on dark fills, The primary and danger buttons in light mode. Not for: Text on the page's own surfaces (use color.text.primary). Sits on: fills of its tone: color.surface.canvas, color.surface.default, color.surface.raised, color.surface.sunken, color.surface.highlight, color.surface.pressed, color.surface.selected, color.surface.inverse, color.action.primary.@, color.action.primary.hover, color.action.danger.@, color.action.danger.hover, color.action.secondary.@, color.action.secondary.hover, color.status.info.subtle, color.status.warning.subtle, color.status.danger.subtle, color.status.success.subtle at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.text.info-on-light: The label on a light info fill, such as its tint in light mode: a fixed color from the light scale (800). Use for: The info badge. Not for: Info text on the page (use color.status.info.@). Sits on: fills of its tone: color.status.info.subtle at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.text.info-on-dark: The label on a dark info fill, such as its tint in dark mode: a fixed color from the light scale (100, adjusted so its hue shows). Use for: The info badge. Not for: Info text on the page (use color.status.info.@). Sits on: fills of its tone: color.status.info.subtle at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.text.success-on-light: The label on a light success fill, such as its tint in light mode: a fixed color from the light scale (800). Use for: The success badge. Not for: Success text on the page (use color.status.success.@). Sits on: fills of its tone: color.status.success.subtle at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.text.success-on-dark: The label on a dark success fill, such as its tint in dark mode: a fixed color from the light scale (100, adjusted so its hue shows). Use for: The success badge. Not for: Success text on the page (use color.status.success.@). Sits on: fills of its tone: color.status.success.subtle at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.text.warning-on-light: The label on a light warning fill, such as its tint in light mode: a fixed color from the light scale (800). Use for: The warning badge. Not for: Warning text on the page (use color.status.warning.@). Sits on: fills of its tone: color.status.warning.subtle at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.text.warning-on-dark: The label on a dark warning fill, such as its tint in dark mode: a fixed color from the light scale (100, adjusted so its hue shows). Use for: The warning badge. Not for: Warning text on the page (use color.status.warning.@). Sits on: fills of its tone: color.status.warning.subtle at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.text.danger-on-light: The label on a light danger fill, such as its tint in light mode: a fixed color from the light scale (800). Use for: The danger badge. Not for: Danger text on the page (use color.status.danger.@). Sits on: fills of its tone: color.status.danger.subtle at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.text.danger-on-dark: The label on a dark danger fill, such as its tint in dark mode: a fixed color from the light scale (100, adjusted so its hue shows). Use for: The danger badge. Not for: Danger text on the page (use color.status.danger.@). Sits on: fills of its tone: color.status.danger.subtle at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.text.on-action: Text and icons on the main action's fill. Use for: Primary button labels. Not for: Text on the page (use color.text.primary). Sits on: color.action.primary.@, color.action.primary.hover at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.text.on-danger: Text on the danger fill: its tone's main text. Use for: The danger button label. Not for: Text on the main action (use color.text.on-action). Sits on: color.action.danger.@, color.action.danger.hover at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.text.link: Links in running text. Use for: Inline links. Not for: Buttons (use color.action.primary.@). Sits on: fills of its tone: color.surface.canvas, color.surface.default, color.surface.raised, color.surface.sunken, color.surface.highlight, color.surface.selected at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.border.default: Quiet edges and dividers. Decorative, so it has no contrast minimum. Use for: Card edges, Dividers, Table rules. Not for: The edge of a control people must find (use color.border.strong).
- color.border.raised: The 1px edge of a raised layer. In dark, a solid step lighter than the raised surface, so the edge shows where a shadow cannot. Use for: Menus, Popovers, Dialogs, Toasts, Raised cards. Not for: Dividers and card borders in the page flow (use color.border.default); The edge of a control people must find (use color.border.strong).
- color.border.strong: The edge of a control people must find. Use for: Input borders, Checkbox borders, Secondary button borders, An edge under the pointer, like the sidebar rail line, A scroll thumb or a resize handle under the pointer or in keyboard focus. Not for: A divider (use color.border.default). Sits on: fills of its tone: color.surface.canvas, color.surface.default, color.surface.raised, color.surface.sunken, color.surface.highlight, color.surface.pressed, color.surface.selected at 3:1 or more.
- color.border.focus: The focus ring. Use for: Keyboard focus on any control. Not for: A selected item (use color.surface.selected). Sits on: fills of its tone: color.surface.canvas, color.surface.default, color.surface.raised, color.surface.sunken, color.surface.highlight, color.surface.pressed, color.surface.selected, color.surface.inverse at 3:1 or more.
- color.border.selected: The edge that marks a selected item, beside its fill, so selection is never color alone. Use for: A selected table row, The current item in a sidebar or menu, A choice that is checked or on, beside its fill. Not for: Keyboard focus (use color.border.focus); The fill of a selected item (use color.surface.selected). Sits on: color.surface.canvas, color.surface.default, color.surface.selected at 3:1 or more.
- color.action.primary.@: The one main action in a view. Use for: Primary button fill, Checked controls, Active tab indicator. Not for: A second action in the same view (use color.action.secondary.@); Links in text (use color.text.link); News or status (use color.status.info.@). Sits on: color.surface.canvas, color.surface.default at 3:1 or more.
- color.action.primary.hover: The main action under the pointer. Use for: Primary button hover. Not for: The resting state (use color.action.primary.@).
- color.action.secondary.@: The fill of other actions. Use for: Secondary buttons. Not for: The main action (use color.action.primary.@).
- color.action.secondary.hover: Other actions under the pointer. Use for: Secondary button hover. Not for: The resting state (use color.action.secondary.@).
- color.action.danger.@: The fill of a destructive commit: the confirm of a delete. Use for: The confirm button of a delete or remove. Not for: The first step of a delete (use color.action.secondary.@); An error message (use color.status.danger.@).
- color.action.danger.hover: The danger fill on hover. Use for: Hover on the danger button. Not for: The resting fill (use color.action.danger.@).
- color.status.info.@: Neutral news: something changed and no action is needed. The lowest level of the urgency order. Use for: Status text and icons. Not for: Something needs a check (use color.status.warning.@); The main action (use color.action.primary.@); The info badge label (use color.text.info-on-light). Sits on: color.surface.canvas, color.surface.default at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.status.info.subtle: The fill behind info status. Use for: Info badges, Banners. Not for: Large page areas (use color.surface.default).
- color.status.warning.@: Caution: something may go wrong or needs a check, and it can be fixed. Use for: Status text and icons. Not for: An error, or an action that cannot be undone (use color.status.danger.@); News that needs no action (use color.status.info.@); The warning badge label (use color.text.warning-on-light). Sits on: color.surface.canvas, color.surface.default at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.status.warning.subtle: The fill behind warning status. Use for: Warning badges, Banners. Not for: Large page areas (use color.surface.default).
- color.status.danger.@: Real risk: errors, failed checks, actions that cannot be undone. The top of the urgency order. Overuse wears it out. Use for: Error messages and status text, Icons. Not for: Caution or advice (use color.status.warning.@); Getting attention (use color.status.info.@); The danger badge label (use color.text.danger-on-light). Sits on: color.surface.canvas, color.surface.default at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.status.danger.subtle: The fill behind danger status. Use for: Danger badges, Banners, Destructive menu items, as the fill behind them, The halo around an invalid field. Not for: Large page areas (use color.surface.default).
- color.status.success.@: Confirmation that something worked. It sits outside the urgency order. Use for: Status text and icons. Not for: The main action (use color.action.primary.@); Brand color (use color.action.primary.@); The success badge label (use color.text.success-on-light). Sits on: color.surface.canvas, color.surface.default at 4.5:1 or more.
- color.status.success.subtle: The fill behind success status. Use for: Success badges, Banners. Not for: Large page areas (use color.surface.default).
- color.category.1.@: Category 1: tells one item or series from another. It carries no meaning. Use for: Chart series, Tag dots and icons. Not for: Status or risk (use color.status.warning.@); Tag text (use color.text.primary). Sits on: color.surface.canvas, color.surface.default at 3:1 or more.
- color.category.1.subtle: Category 1: the fill of a tag. Use for: Tag and label fills. Not for: A status badge (use color.status.info.subtle).
- color.category.2.@: Category 2: tells one item or series from another. It carries no meaning. Use for: Chart series, Tag dots and icons. Not for: Status or risk (use color.status.warning.@); Tag text (use color.text.primary). Sits on: color.surface.canvas, color.surface.default at 3:1 or more.
- color.category.2.subtle: Category 2: the fill of a tag. Use for: Tag and label fills. Not for: A status badge (use color.status.info.subtle).
- color.category.3.@: Category 3: tells one item or series from another. It carries no meaning. Use for: Chart series, Tag dots and icons. Not for: Status or risk (use color.status.warning.@); Tag text (use color.text.primary). Sits on: color.surface.canvas, color.surface.default at 3:1 or more.
- color.category.3.subtle: Category 3: the fill of a tag. Use for: Tag and label fills. Not for: A status badge (use color.status.info.subtle).
- color.category.4.@: Category 4: tells one item or series from another. It carries no meaning. Use for: Chart series, Tag dots and icons. Not for: Status or risk (use color.status.warning.@); Tag text (use color.text.primary). Sits on: color.surface.canvas, color.surface.default at 3:1 or more.
- color.category.4.subtle: Category 4: the fill of a tag. Use for: Tag and label fills. Not for: A status badge (use color.status.info.subtle).
- color.category.5.@: Category 5: tells one item or series from another. It carries no meaning. Use for: Chart series, Tag dots and icons. Not for: Status or risk (use color.status.warning.@); Tag text (use color.text.primary). Sits on: color.surface.canvas, color.surface.default at 3:1 or more.
- color.category.5.subtle: Category 5: the fill of a tag. Use for: Tag and label fills. Not for: A status badge (use color.status.info.subtle).
- color.disabled.text: Text and icons of a control that cannot be used right now. Use for: Disabled labels and icons. Not for: Quiet text that still works (use color.text.muted). Sits on: color.disabled.surface.
- color.disabled.surface: The fill of a control that cannot be used right now. Use for: Disabled buttons and inputs. Not for: A quiet fill that still works (use color.surface.sunken).
- color.disabled.border: The edge of a control that cannot be used right now. Use for: Disabled inputs and checkboxes. Not for: An enabled control (use color.border.strong).

## Accessible first (accessible-first)

Accessible first is an Open DS scheme: a full set of answers to the Open DS grammar, with the reasons behind each, usage rules, voice and tone, and the tokens that follow. Large text, large targets and AAA contrast for the text you must read, so everyone can finish the task.

Use when: Public services, health, government and any product that must work for everyone.
Avoid when: Dense expert tools where screen space matters more than size.
Themes: light, dark

### Answers

- business.q1 What does the product do for the business? Serves the public. A public service everyone must be able to use.
- business.q2 How many brands or products share the system? One. One service, one brand.
- people.q1 Who uses it most? Everyone, including people with disabilities. Everyone, including people with low vision, motor and cognitive needs. (because business.q1)
- people.q2 What accessibility level do we commit to? AAA. AAA where it applies; nobody is left out. (because people.q1)
- content.q1 What is the main content? Forms and tasks. Most screens are forms and steps. (because business.q1)
- content.q2 How much is on one screen? One idea at a time. One question per screen lowers effort. (because people.q1)
- tasks.q1 What is the main task? Complete a form. People must finish the form. (because content.q1)
- tasks.q2 How often do people repeat actions? Rarely. People do this once or twice a year. (because business.q1)
- human.q1 What must the interface protect? Low effort to understand. Low effort to understand each step. (because people.q1)
- human.q2 How do people recall the interface? They see it fresh each time. Nobody remembers the interface from last time. (because tasks.q2)
- outcomes.q1 Which outcome matters most? Completion without errors. Completion without errors is the measure. (because tasks.q1)
- outcomes.q2 What is a costly mistake? A task that fails. A failed form can cost someone a benefit. (because tasks.q1)
- brand.q1 What should the brand feel like? Calm and clear. Calm and clear, never clever. (because human.q1)
- brand.q2 How visible is the brand in the interface? Quiet. The brand stays out of the way. (because human.q1)
- brand.q3 Which typefaces carry the product, and why? One face drawn for legibility. Atkinson Hyperlegible for everything: it was drawn so letters can't be mistaken, and nobody is left out. (because brand.q1, people.q2, content.q1)
- scenarios.q1 Where do people use it? Anywhere, on any device. Public services are used on any device, with any assistive technology. (because people.q1)
- scenarios.q2 How long is one visit? One sitting. An application is finished in one sitting, or saved and resumed. (because tasks.q1)
- team.q1 Who maintains the system? A platform team. A platform team serves many services.
- team.q2 How fast does it change? Rarely. Changes are rare and tested.
- typography.roles Which text roles does it need? Core: heading, body, label. Few roles keep pages predictable. (because human.q1)
- typography.count How many steps does the type scale take? Only the steps the screens need. Only the sizes the screens need, each clearly different. (because human.q1)
- typography.definition How are sizes and line heights defined? A ratio, line heights in proportion. Line height grows with text size for zoom users. (because people.q2)
- typography.values How large is body text? Large. Large text is readable for more people. (because people.q1)
- typography.lands Where does type do the most work? Forms and labels. Type matters most in form labels and hints. (because content.q1)
- color.roles Which color roles does it need? Surface, text, action and status. Few color roles, each with one clear meaning. (because human.q1)
- color.count How many emphasis levels do actions need? Two. Primary and secondary only; fewer choices, fewer errors. (because human.q1)
- color.definition How is the palette defined? Neutrals and one brand ramp. True neutrals and blue 600 as the brand: the familiar web color of links and focus, AAA with white text, and clear to color-blind users. (because people.q2, people.q1, color.lands)
- color.values How saturated is the palette? Balanced. Strong but not loud color. (because brand.q1)
- color.lands Where does color carry meaning first? Links and actions. Links and actions must be found by everyone. (because outcomes.q1)
- spacing.roles Which spacing roles does it need? Gaps, insets and row heights. Large rows matter for touch and zoom. (because people.q1)
- spacing.count How many densities exist? One. One density; no compact mode to fail people. (because people.q1)
- spacing.definition How are spacing steps defined? Big, even steps. Big, even steps lower effort. (because human.q1)
- spacing.values How dense is the layout? Spacious. Space lowers effort and mis-taps. (because human.q1)
- spacing.lands Where does spacing matter most? Between fields. Space between fields prevents mis-taps. (because content.q1)
- shape.roles Which shape roles does it need? Controls, badges and containers. Badges keep a clear rectangle. (because human.q1)
- shape.count How many corner sizes exist? Three. Control, badge and container corners differ. (because shape.roles)
- shape.definition How are corners set? Fixed for the product. One brand, one set of corners. (because business.q2)
- shape.values What should control corners say? Slightly rounded. Clear, slightly rounded controls. (because brand.q1)
- shape.lands Where does shape show most? Controls and cards. Corners show on controls and step cards. (because content.q1)
- elevation.roles What rises above the page? Nothing. Flat is easier to read at high zoom. (because people.q2)
- elevation.count How many shadow levels exist? None. No shadows. (because elevation.roles)
- elevation.definition What separates groups on the page? Lines. Strong borders separate groups at any zoom. (because people.q2)
- elevation.values How soft are shadows? No shadows. No shadows; borders do the work. (because elevation.roles)
- elevation.lands Where does elevation show? Dialogs only. Only dialogs separate, with a dimmed page and a border. (because elevation.roles)
- motion.roles What is motion for? Feedback only. Motion only confirms an action. (because people.q1)
- motion.count How many speeds exist? One. One speed. (because motion.roles)
- motion.definition How is easing defined? Standard ease-out. A standard ease-out is easy to follow. (because people.q1)
- motion.values How fast does feedback feel? Moderate. Moderate speed is easy to follow. (because people.q1)
- motion.lands Where does motion show? State changes only. Only state changes move. (because motion.roles)
- iconography.roles What do icons do? Actions and status. Icons support words; they never replace them. (because human.q2)
- iconography.count How many icon sizes exist? One. One size, larger than the text. (because iconography.values)
- iconography.definition What icon style and stroke? Bold stroke. A bold 2px stroke keeps every icon easy to see, for low vision and small screens. (because people.q1)
- iconography.values How big are icons next to text? Larger than the text. Larger icons are easier to see. (because people.q1)
- iconography.lands Where do icons work hardest? Status and messages. Icons work hardest beside status words and errors. (because accessibility.count)
- theming.roles What can a theme change? Mode only. One brand, so only the mode changes. (because business.q2)
- theming.count How many themes ship? Two. Light and dark. (because theming.values)
- theming.definition How are brands handled? One brand. One service, one brand. (because business.q2)
- theming.values Which modes ship? Light and dark. Light and dark ship as standard; both hold AAA text. (because people.q2)
- theming.lands What changes when the theme changes? Colors only. Only colors change. (because theming.roles)
- accessibility.roles Which states get their own visible value? All, including loading. Every state, including loading, gets its own value. (because people.q2)
- accessibility.count How many signals carry each meaning? Three: color, icon and word. Never color alone. (because people.q2)
- accessibility.definition What contrast floor do we hold? AAA for text. AAA for text you must read; AA for muted text, which must look secondary. Muted text on the canvas is the owner's recorded exception. (because people.q2)
- accessibility.values What is the smallest target? Large. Large targets for tremor and touch. (because people.q1)
- accessibility.lands Where are the floors hardest to hold? Forms. Forms are where people are blocked. (because content.q1)
- naming.roles What gets a name? Tokens and component keys. Components get their own keys. (because team.q2)
- naming.count How many token tiers? Three. Primitives, semantics and component keys. (because team.q2)
- naming.definition How are decisions named? By role. Role names survive a redesign. (because team.q1)
- naming.values How are names written? Lowercase words in paths. Lowercase paths read the same everywhere. (because team.q1)
- naming.lands What do components read? Component keys. A component API keeps changes local. (because team.q2)
- voice.roles Which kinds of copy does it need? Labels, messages and help. Hints and help text carry people through each step. (because content.q1)
- voice.count How many tones does it use? One. One plain tone everywhere; no surprises. (because human.q1)
- voice.definition How is the voice defined? Rules and a word list. A word list of common words, with terms to avoid. (because people.q1)
- voice.values How does it sound? Plain and direct. Every sentence is easy to read on the first try. (because people.q1, brand.q1)
- voice.lands Where do the words matter most? Form steps and errors. Words decide whether a form gets finished. (because outcomes.q1)
- components.roles Which component families does it need? Actions, forms, feedback, overlays, layout and navigation. Forms, steps and feedback are all a public service needs. (because content.q1, people.q1)
- components.count How far does the inventory reach? Only what today's screens use. Only the parts in use, each tested with assistive technology. (because people.q2, team.q2)
- components.definition How does a component earn its place? It works for everyone, with any device and assistive technology. A component joins only when it works with any device and assistive technology. (because people.q1, people.q2)
- components.values When does a component get another look? Only when the meaning changes. One clear way to do each thing. (because people.q1, brand.q1)
- components.lands Where do components do the most work? Forms and steps. Components do their work in forms and steps. (because content.q1, tasks.q1)

### Usage rules

- Page title (page-title): use type.title; not type.display; The same title size on every page tells people where they are. The display size changes from page to page and pushes the content down.
- A number in a table (number-in-table): use type.body; not A small or mono font; Every number must be readable at large size.
- Paragraph or help text (paragraph): use type.body, short sentences; not type.caption; Large text and short lines lower effort.
- Field label or column header (field-label): use type.label, above the field, always visible; not A placeholder as the label; Labels must stay visible while typing.
- A selected row or item (selected-row): use color.surface.selected and a check icon; not Color alone; Selection never relies on color alone.
- An error message (error-message): use color.status.danger, an icon and a sentence next to the field; not Color alone; People must know what went wrong and where.
- A link (link): use color.text.link, underlined; not Color only; Underline works without color perception.
- A status (status-label): use Badge with an icon and a word; not Color alone; Status must survive no color and a screen reader.
- Items that belong together (related-items): use space.gap.default; not space.gap.tight; Items in one group sit 16px apart, not the 12px tight gap: generous space between fields stops mis-taps.
- Between page sections (between-sections): use space.gap.section; not A thin line; Space is easy to see; thin lines are not.
- Table row height (table-row): use size.row (large); not A compact row; Large rows are easy to read and tap.
- Corners of buttons and inputs (control-corner): use radius.control; not A pill; Clear rectangles read as fields and buttons.
- Shape of a status badge (status-shape): use radius.badge (rectangle); not A pill; Clear shapes with a word inside.
- A card on the page (card): use A strong border, no shadow; not A shadow; Shadows are hard to see; borders are not.
- A menu or dialog (menu-or-dialog): use A strong border and a dimmed page; not A shadow only; The dimmed page makes the dialog obvious.
- Hover and press feedback (hover-feedback): use motion.duration.feedback (moderate); not Fast flicker; Moderate speed is easy to follow.
- Someone asked for less motion (reduced-motion): use Fades only; nothing moves; not Reduced motion; Movement can make some people dizzy, so it stops. A short fade or a color change still shows that something changed.
- An icon with no label (icon-alone): use Not used: always add a word; not An icon button; Icons alone are guesswork.
- Someone switches to dark (dark-mode): use The dark semantic mode, or high contrast; not One mode only; People pick the mode they can read.
- Keyboard focus (keyboard-focus): use button/focus-ring at focus.ring.width, with an offset; not A thin or faint outline; Focus must be seen by everyone.
- The smallest clickable thing (smallest-target): use size.control.default (large); not Touch-minimum size; Large targets help people with motor needs.
- The action that completes the task (commit-action): use Button primary, one per page; not Two primaries; One clear next step. Two primaries make people stop and compare, which adds effort.
- An alternative or cancel (alternative-action): use Button secondary; not A text link; Every action looks like a button people can find.
- Delete or remove (destructive-action): use Button secondary, then a confirm page with Button danger; not Button primary; A confirm step prevents a costly error.
- An action on one row or item (row-action): use Button secondary with a word; not An icon on its own; A word says what will happen.
- A value with no token (missing-token): use The closest semantic token, then ask for a new one; not A raw value in the component; A raw value skips the contrast checks every token passed.
- A button label (button-label): use A common verb that says what happens next; not "Submit" or "Proceed"; Common words are understood by the most people. Example: "Continue"
- The words of an error (error-words): use Say what is wrong, where, and exactly how to fix it; not "Invalid input"; People must be able to fix the error without help. Example: "Enter your date of birth. For example, 27 3 1980."
- A success message (success-words): use Confirm what happened and what comes next; not A confirmation with no next step; People need to know the task is finished and what happens now. Example: "We have your application. We will email you within 5 working days."
- An empty state (empty-words): use Explain what will appear here and how to start; not A blank page; A blank page leaves people unsure if something failed. Example: "You have no saved applications. Start a new one below."
- A confirmation question (confirm-words): use Say what will happen in plain words, and offer a way back; not A double negative; Plain words prevent a choice people did not mean. Example: "Do you want to cancel your application? Your answers will be deleted."
- A first visit (first-visit): use Say how many steps there are and how long it takes; not Marketing copy; Knowing the length lowers effort and anxiety. Example: "This takes about 10 minutes. There are 4 steps."
- No component in the inventory fits (missing-component): use a native HTML element with a label and a hint; not a custom widget that needs hover, drag or precise pointing; Native elements work with every assistive technology without extra work.
- Hero line or key number (hero-line): use type.display; not type.display on step pages; It is for the one headline on the start page. The start page says what the service does in one big line. Every step after it uses the title size.
- Section heading (section-heading): use type.heading; not Bold body text; Clear headings split a page into short parts that people can find again.
- Supporting text (supporting-text): use type.caption; not type.caption for a hint sentence; It is for a few short words only; a sentence uses type.body. Small text is harder to read. A hint that people must follow gets body size.
- Text in a table cell (table-cell): use type.data; not A small or mono font; It equals body here. Every cell stays as large and plain as body text, for people with low vision.
- Title of a form page (form-page-title): use type.title; not type.display; Every step page has the same title size, so people always know where they are.
- Parts of one item (parts-of-one-item): use space.gap.tight; not No gap; Parts sit close enough to read as one item, with room to tell them apart at high zoom.
- Items in a list or a form row (siblings-in-a-row): use space.gap.default; not space.gap.tight; Space between fields lowers mis-taps for people with tremor.
- Between groups (between-groups): use space.gap.group; not space.gap.default; A clear break shows where one group of questions ends and the next begins.
- Inside a button or input (inside-a-control): use space.inset.control-x; not Padding set by eye; Wide padding makes each button a bigger target that is easy to hit.
- Inside a card, panel or dialog (inside-a-container): use space.inset.container; not Text that touches the edge; Wide padding keeps content clear of the strong border at any zoom.
- Inside a table cell (inside-a-cell): use space.inset.cell-x; not Narrow cell padding; Clear space between columns keeps values apart at high zoom.
- An option in a menu or list (option-in-list): use radius.option; not radius.control; The option corner nests inside the menu, so the highlighted option reads as one clear box.
- Something that grows past one line (growing-element): use radius.element; not radius.surface; Text areas and list items keep the control corner, so people know they can type or pick there.
- Corners of cards, menus and dialogs (surface-corner): use radius.surface; not A pill; Slightly rounded panels read as one clear box at any zoom.
- Edges and dividers (edges-and-dividers): use border-width.default; not A hairline; A strong edge stays visible at high zoom and for people with low vision.
- The gap around a focus ring (focus-gap): use focus.ring.offset; not A ring that touches the control; The gap keeps the thick ring clear of the control, so focus shows on any fill.
- A panel opens (panel-opens): use motion.duration.panels; not A long slide; A moderate open is easy to follow and shows where the panel came from.
- The curve of any move (any-transition): use motion.easing.standard; not A spring that overshoots; A plain ease-out is calm and clear. An overshoot can confuse and distract.
- A hero or launch moment (hero-motion): use No hero motion; not An animated start page; Moving content distracts people with attention needs and slows the task.
- An icon beside text (icon-beside-text): use size.icon and icon.stroke-width; not A thin icon at text size; Larger icons with a bold line stay easy to see for people with low vision.
- Most buttons and inputs (most-controls): use size.control.default; not A touch-minimum size; Large controls help people with tremor and low vision.
- The main action on a screen (main-action): use size.control.large; not A taller button for the main action; It is the same height as the default here. Every control is already large. One height on every button keeps pages predictable.
- A button inside a field (control-inside-field): use size.control.compact; not A small icon button; It still meets the large target size and fits inside the field.
- A control that is not available yet (unavailable-control): use color.disabled.*, never opacity; not A faded control with no reason; Muted colors keep the label readable, where a fade would drop its contrast. A hint says what is missing and the next step.

### Voice and tone

Plain and direct. Every sentence is easy to read on the first try. (follows voice.values, people.q1)
- Use common words. Explain any term you must use. (follows voice.definition, people.q1)
- One idea per sentence. Put the action first. (follows human.q1)
- Never blame the person. (follows voice.values)
- A button label stays on one line: it never breaks onto two. (follows voice.values, voice.definition)
Use: Continue, Change, Start, You. Avoid: Invalid, Utilise, Submit, Error code.
The tone per moment is in the usage rules of the voice situations above.

### Use scenarios

- A person with low vision zooms to 200% and applies for a benefit with a screen magnifier. (follows scenarios.q1, people.q1, people.q2)
- A person with a tremor completes a form on a tablet. (follows scenarios.q1, scenarios.q2, tasks.q1)

## Brand expressive (brand-expressive)

Brand expressive is an Open DS scheme: a full set of answers to the Open DS grammar, with the reasons behind each, usage rules, voice and tone, and the tokens that follow. Big display type, vivid color and springy motion, for launches that must be remembered.

Use when: Launch sites, campaigns, marketing pages and consumer brands that lead with personality.
Avoid when: Tools people use for hours, or forms where calm matters more than character.
Themes: light, dark

### Answers

- business.q1 What does the product do for the business? Sells and converts. A launch site that must win attention and sign-ups.
- business.q2 How many brands or products share the system? One. One brand, loudly.
- people.q1 Who uses it most? Customers who choose us. New customers deciding if they care. (because business.q1)
- people.q2 What accessibility level do we commit to? AA. AA, even when loud. (because people.q1)
- content.q1 What is the main content? Images and campaigns. Images, campaigns and short punchy copy. (because business.q1)
- content.q2 How much is on one screen? One idea at a time. One big idea per section. (because content.q1)
- tasks.q1 What is the main task? Browse and explore. People browse and explore the story. (because content.q1)
- tasks.q2 How often do people repeat actions? Rarely. One action: sign up. (because business.q1)
- human.q1 What must the interface protect? Delight. Delight is the point. (because business.q1)
- human.q2 How do people recall the interface? They see it fresh each time. Every visit should feel fresh. (because people.q1)
- outcomes.q1 Which outcome matters most? Engagement. Engagement and sign-ups. (because business.q1)
- outcomes.q2 What is a costly mistake? Looking off-brand. A bland page is the costly mistake. (because business.q1)
- brand.q1 What should the brand feel like? Bold. Bold and confident. (because business.q1)
- brand.q2 How visible is the brand in the interface? Loud. The brand is loud everywhere. (because brand.q1)
- brand.q3 Which typefaces carry the product, and why? A display face for brand moments, with a sans for text. Bricolage Grotesque for display and headings, DM Sans for text: loud where the brand speaks, easy where people read. (because brand.q1, brand.q2, content.q1)
- scenarios.q1 Where do people use it? On the move. Visitors come from social posts on their phones. (because people.q1)
- scenarios.q2 How long is one visit? A few minutes. A visit lasts a few minutes at most. (because outcomes.q1)
- team.q1 Who maintains the system? An agency. An agency runs campaigns.
- team.q2 How fast does it change? Every campaign. Every campaign changes the look a little. (because team.q1)
- typography.roles Which text roles does it need? Core and expressive display. A big expressive display role carries the brand. (because brand.q2)
- typography.count How many steps does the type scale take? Fine steps, so pages can set their own rhythm. Fine steps give big moments room. (because brand.q2)
- typography.definition How are sizes and line heights defined? A ratio, line heights in proportion. Ratios suit the big display sizes. (because typography.roles)
- typography.values How large is body text? Regular. Regular body; the display does the shouting. (because content.q2)
- typography.lands Where does type do the most work? Headlines and hero. Type does its work in headlines. (because brand.q2)
- color.roles Which color roles does it need? Those and brand accents. Brand accents are part of the message. (because brand.q2)
- color.count How many emphasis levels do actions need? Three. Primary, secondary, ghost. (because tasks.q2)
- color.definition How is the palette defined? Neutrals and one brand ramp. Warm neutrals and one vivid ramp. (because brand.q1)
- color.values How saturated is the palette? Vivid. Vivid color is the brand. (because brand.q2)
- color.lands Where does color carry meaning first? Brand moments. Color makes the launch moment. (because outcomes.q1)
- spacing.roles Which spacing roles does it need? Gaps and insets. Few tables; no row role needed. (because content.q1)
- spacing.count How many densities exist? One. One generous density. (because content.q2)
- spacing.definition How are spacing steps defined? Big, even steps. Big, even steps make big moments. (because brand.q2)
- spacing.values How dense is the layout? Spacious. Big space makes big moments. (because content.q2)
- spacing.lands Where does spacing matter most? Between big sections. Space works between big sections. (because content.q1)
- shape.roles Which shape roles does it need? Controls and containers. Pills everywhere; badges share the control corner. (because brand.q1)
- shape.count How many corner sizes exist? Two. Pill controls and large container corners. (because shape.roles)
- shape.definition How are corners set? Fixed for the product. One brand, one set of corners. (because business.q2)
- shape.values What should control corners say? Pill. Pill controls feel playful. (because brand.q1)
- shape.lands Where does shape show most? Buttons and badges. Pill buttons are the signature shape. (because brand.q2)
- elevation.roles What rises above the page? Cards too. Cards lift to feel like objects. (because brand.q2)
- elevation.count How many shadow levels exist? Two. One shadow for cards, one for overlays. (because elevation.roles)
- elevation.definition What separates groups on the page? Cards. Cards hold each offer. (because content.q1)
- elevation.values How soft are shadows? Pronounced. Pronounced shadows add depth. (because brand.q2)
- elevation.lands Where does elevation show? Cards, menus and dialogs. Cards, menus and dialogs rise. (because elevation.roles)
- motion.roles What is motion for? Feedback and expression. Motion carries personality. (because brand.q2)
- motion.count How many speeds exist? Three. Fast feedback, moderate panels, relaxed hero. (because motion.roles)
- motion.definition How is easing defined? A spring. A spring that overshoots feels alive. (because brand.q1)
- motion.values How fast does feedback feel? Fast. Feedback stays fast; the personality shows in panels and hero moments, which move slower on a spring. (because human.q1)
- motion.lands Where does motion show? Hero and launch moments. Motion shows in hero and launch moments. (because outcomes.q1)
- iconography.roles What do icons do? Those and decoration. Icons also decorate campaign pages. (because brand.q2)
- iconography.count How many icon sizes exist? Two. One size next to text, one for decoration. (because iconography.roles)
- iconography.definition What icon style and stroke? Contained. Contained icons sit in a tinted shape at a 1.75px stroke, so they carry the brand's warmth. (because color.values)
- iconography.values How big are icons next to text? Larger than the text. Larger icons hold their own next to big type. (because typography.roles)
- iconography.lands Where do icons work hardest? Buttons and calls to action. Icons sit in calls to action. (because outcomes.q1)
- theming.roles What can a theme change? Mode only. One brand, so only the mode changes. (because business.q2)
- theming.count How many themes ship? Two. Light and dark. (because theming.values)
- theming.definition How are brands handled? One brand. One brand per campaign. (because business.q2)
- theming.values Which modes ship? Light and dark. Light and dark ship as standard. (because people.q1)
- theming.lands What changes when the theme changes? Colors only. Only colors change. (because theming.roles)
- accessibility.roles Which states get their own visible value? Those and pressed. Pressed for touch. (because accessibility.values)
- accessibility.count How many signals carry each meaning? Two: color and word. Color and word. (because people.q2)
- accessibility.definition What contrast floor do we hold? AA. AA, checked on every vivid color. (because people.q2)
- accessibility.values What is the smallest target? Touch size. Visitors come from social posts on phones. (because scenarios.q1)
- accessibility.lands Where are the floors hardest to hold? Brand color. Vivid brand color is the hardest to keep readable. (because color.values)
- naming.roles What gets a name? Tokens and component keys. Components get their own keys. (because team.q2)
- naming.count How many token tiers? Three. Primitives, semantics and component keys. (because team.q2)
- naming.definition How are decisions named? By role. Role names survive each campaign. (because team.q2)
- naming.values How are names written? Lowercase words in paths. Lowercase paths read the same everywhere. (because team.q1)
- naming.lands What do components read? Component keys. Campaigns change primitives, never components. (because team.q2)
- voice.roles Which kinds of copy does it need? Labels, messages and headlines. Headlines carry the campaign. (because business.q1)
- voice.count How many tones does it use? One per moment. Playful in headlines, plain in errors. (because outcomes.q2)
- voice.definition How is the voice defined? Principles and examples. Principles and examples guide each campaign's writers. (because team.q1)
- voice.values How does it sound? Playful. Big words, few of them. (because brand.q1, brand.q2)
- voice.lands Where do the words matter most? Headlines and buttons. Words work hardest in headlines and buttons. (because outcomes.q1)
- components.roles Which component families does it need? Core, plus media. Campaigns lead with media and big sections. (because content.q1, brand.q2)
- components.count How far does the inventory reach? Only what today's screens use. One action and a story need only the parts in use; an agency keeps them fresh. (because tasks.q2, team.q1)
- components.definition How does a component earn its place? It gives the brand a moment. A component joins when it gives the campaign a moment. (because brand.q1, outcomes.q1)
- components.values When does a component get another look? Also for emphasis and size. Variants for emphasis and size let each campaign look a little different. (because team.q2, brand.q2)
- components.lands Where do components do the most work? Campaign sections. Components sit inside big campaign sections. (because content.q1, tasks.q1)

### Usage rules

- Page title (page-title): use type.display; not type.title; The display role carries the brand in every hero.
- A number in a table (number-in-table): use type.body; not A mono font; Tables are rare and never compared column by column, so mono digits add nothing. The brand font keeps the voice.
- Paragraph or help text (paragraph): use type.body, short; not Long paragraphs; Short copy keeps the energy.
- Field label or column header (field-label): use type.label; not type.caption; Labels stay readable on vivid color.
- A selected row or item (selected-row): use color.surface.selected (brand tint); not Grey; Selection carries the brand.
- An error message (error-message): use color.status.danger and a short sentence; not The brand magenta; Errors must not look like the brand.
- A link (link): use color.text.link, underlined; not Color only; Underline keeps links clear on vivid color.
- A status (status-label): use Badge pill with a word; not Color alone; A word keeps meaning on vivid backgrounds.
- Items that belong together (related-items): use space.gap.default; not space.gap.tight; Air keeps big type readable.
- Between page sections (between-sections): use space.gap.section and a color block; not A thin line; Big space and color make each section a moment.
- Table row height (table-row): use size.row (comfortable); not A compact row; Tables are rare and short, so there is no need to fit many rows. Comfortable rows keep the brand's airy rhythm.
- Corners of buttons and inputs (control-corner): use radius.control (pill); not Sharp corners; Pills match the brand's round, playful shapes. Sharp corners would feel corporate.
- Shape of a status badge (status-shape): use radius.badge (pill); not A rectangle; Pills match the controls.
- A card on the page (card): use elevation.card (pronounced); none in dark; not A flat card; Cards float to feel tactile. In dark a shade cannot be seen, so a lighter surface and a light ring lift them.
- A menu or dialog (menu-or-dialog): use elevation.overlay and a dimmed page; not No shadow; Strong depth shows a menu or dialog sits above vivid sections. Without a shadow it blends into the color blocks.
- Hover and press feedback (hover-feedback): use motion.duration.feedback (fast); not An instant change; Fast feedback on an ease-out. The brand's spring waits for the moments that deserve it.
- Someone asked for less motion (reduced-motion): use Fades only; nothing moves; not Full motion; Motion is part of the brand, so it shrinks to a fade instead of vanishing. Full motion is never forced on people who asked for less.
- An icon with no label (icon-alone): use Not used: always add a word; not An icon button with a hover hint; On phones, hover hints never show; a word says what will happen.
- Someone switches to dark (dark-mode): use The dark semantic mode; not A separate campaign palette; Dark ships as standard; campaigns change values, not structure.
- Keyboard focus (keyboard-focus): use button/focus-ring at focus.ring.width; not Removing the outline; Focus must show on vivid color.
- The smallest clickable thing (smallest-target): use size.control.default (touch); not A compact control; Most visitors arrive on phones, and a compact control is too small for a thumb.
- The action that completes the task (commit-action): use Button primary, large, one per section; not Two primaries; One loud call to action per section.
- An alternative or cancel (alternative-action): use Button ghost; not A second primary; The alternative must not compete.
- Delete or remove (destructive-action): use Button secondary, then confirm with Button danger; not Button primary; Confirm before destroying data.
- An action on one row or item (row-action): use Button ghost with a word; not An icon alone; Visitors come rarely, so they never learn an icon. A word says what will happen.
- A value with no token (missing-token): use The closest semantic token, then ask for a new one; not A raw value in the component; The next campaign changes primitives; raw values would stay behind.
- A button label (button-label): use A short verb that moves: Join, Try, Go; not "Learn more"; Big moments need verbs with energy. Example: "Join the drop"
- The words of an error (error-words): use Plain first, a light touch after; not A joke before the fix; Playful copy must never hide what went wrong. Example: "That email doesn't look right. Check it and try again."
- A success message (success-words): use Celebrate, briefly; not A long thank-you; A short celebration is remembered. Example: "You're on the list. See you at launch."
- An empty state (empty-words): use Playful, with a clear next step; not A dead end; Playful words still need a way forward. Example: "Nothing here yet. Go find something you love."
- A confirmation question (confirm-words): use Plain. No jokes when something is lost.; not Playful copy; Loss is never the moment for a joke. Example: "Remove this from your list? You can add it back later."
- A first visit (first-visit): use One bold line and one button; not A paragraph of copy; Visitors from a social post give a few seconds. Example: "The drop is coming. Be first."
- No component in the inventory fits (missing-component): use a section built from the inventory with campaign tokens; not a new component for one campaign; Campaigns change the look through tokens; new parts every drop are hard to keep working.
- Hero line or key number (hero-line): use type.display; not type.title; It is for every hero and section opener. Each section is one big idea. The biggest line sells it in the brand's loudest voice.
- Section heading (section-heading): use type.heading; not Bold body text; Headings carry the brand's display face into cards and dialogs.
- Supporting text (supporting-text): use type.caption; not type.body; Fine print stays small, so the headlines keep the attention that wins sign-ups.
- Text in a table cell (table-cell): use type.data; not A mono font; It equals body here. Tables are rare and short. Cells keep the brand's text face, so they sound like the rest of the page.
- Title of a form page (form-page-title): use type.title; not type.display; The sign-up form is the one action. A smaller title keeps the form in view on a phone.
- Parts of one item (parts-of-one-item): use space.gap.tight; not space.gap.default; An icon and its word sit close, so a call to action reads as one bold unit.
- Items in a list or a form row (siblings-in-a-row): use space.gap.default; not space.gap.tight; Air between items keeps big type readable.
- Between groups (between-groups): use space.gap.group; not space.gap.default; Big gaps give each group its own moment inside a section.
- Inside a button or input (inside-a-control): use space.inset.control-x; not Padding set by eye; Wide padding makes pill buttons bold and easy to hit with a thumb.
- Inside a card, panel or dialog (inside-a-container): use space.inset.container; not Text that touches the card edge; Generous padding lets each card hold its moment.
- Inside a table cell (inside-a-cell): use space.inset.cell-x; not Narrow cell padding; Tables are rare, so cells keep the page's airy rhythm.
- An option in a menu or list (option-in-list): use radius.option; not radius.control; Round options nest inside the round menu, so a menu feels as playful as the buttons.
- Something that grows past one line (growing-element): use radius.element; not radius.control; A pill corner breaks when a text area grows to many lines. The element corner stays round at any height.
- Corners of cards, menus and dialogs (surface-corner): use radius.surface; not Small corners; Big round corners make cards feel like friendly objects.
- Edges and dividers (edges-and-dividers): use border-width.default; not A hairline; A bold edge matches the bold type and vivid color.
- The gap around a focus ring (focus-gap): use focus.ring.offset; not A ring that touches the control; The gap keeps the ring visible on vivid fills.
- A panel opens (panel-opens): use motion.duration.panels; not A flat fade; Panels open on an ease-out at a moderate speed, so menus feel quick and the brand shows in its big moments.
- The curve of any move (any-transition): use motion.easing.standard; not A plain ease-out; An ease-out keeps every menu and button quick. The overshoot is kept for emphasis, where it feels alive and playful.
- A hero or launch moment (hero-motion): use motion.duration.hero; not motion.duration.panels; Hero and launch moments move slowest, so every visitor sees the launch.
- An icon beside text (icon-beside-text): use size.icon and icon.stroke-width; not A thin icon at text size; Larger icons hold their own next to big type. The thicker line carries the brand's warmth.
- Most buttons and inputs (most-controls): use size.control.default; not size.control.compact; Most visitors arrive on phones, so every control fits a thumb.
- The main action on a screen (main-action): use size.control.large; not size.control.default; The sign-up button is the one loud call to action. A bigger button wins the eye and the thumb.
- A button inside a field (control-inside-field): use size.control.compact; not A small icon button; It still fits a thumb and sits inside the pill field.
- A control that is not available yet (unavailable-control): use color.disabled.*, never opacity; not Hiding the button; Muted colors keep the layout and the label readable. The vivid color returns when the visitor can sign up.

### Voice and tone

Playful and short. Big words, few of them. (follows voice.values)
- Headlines are short and bold. Three to six words. (follows voice.lands, typography.roles)
- Verbs that move: Join, Try, Go. (follows voice.values)
- Playful in headlines, plain in errors. (follows voice.count)
- A button label stays on one line: it never breaks onto two. (follows voice.values, voice.definition)
Use: Join, Drop, Go, Love. Avoid: Synergy, Leverage, Kindly.
The tone per moment is in the usage rules of the voice situations above.

### Use scenarios

- A visitor lands on a launch page from a social post and joins the waiting list. (follows scenarios.q1, scenarios.q2, outcomes.q1)
- An agency swaps the campaign colors for the next drop without changing the components. (follows team.q1, team.q2)

## Content first (content-first)

Content first is an Open DS scheme: a full set of answers to the Open DS grammar, with the reasons behind each, usage rules, voice and tone, and the tokens that follow. Large, calm type and generous space, for people who come to read.

Use when: Publications, documentation, blogs, guides and help centers.
Avoid when: Data-heavy tools or screens with many actions.
Themes: light, dark

### Answers

- business.q1 What does the product do for the business? Informs and publishes. The product publishes articles and guides.
- business.q2 How many brands or products share the system? One. One publication, one brand.
- people.q1 Who uses it most? Occasional visitors. Most readers arrive from search and visit now and then. (because business.q1)
- people.q2 What accessibility level do we commit to? AA. AA is the commitment for a public site. (because people.q1)
- content.q1 What is the main content? Long-form text. The content is long-form text. (because business.q1)
- content.q2 How much is on one screen? One idea at a time. One idea per screen keeps reading calm. (because content.q1)
- tasks.q1 What is the main task? Read start to end. People read from start to end. (because content.q1)
- tasks.q2 How often do people repeat actions? Rarely. Actions are rare: subscribe, share, save. (because tasks.q1)
- human.q1 What must the interface protect? Attention on the content. Attention belongs to the text. (because tasks.q1)
- human.q2 How do people recall the interface? They see it fresh each time. Visitors see the interface fresh each time. (because people.q1)
- outcomes.q1 Which outcome matters most? Reading comfort. Comfortable reading is the measure. (because tasks.q1)
- outcomes.q2 What is a costly mistake? Losing your place. Losing your place in an article breaks the read. (because tasks.q1)
- brand.q1 What should the brand feel like? Warm. Warm and considered, like a good magazine. (because business.q1)
- brand.q2 How visible is the brand in the interface? Present. The brand shows in type, not in color. (because brand.q1)
- brand.q3 Which typefaces carry the product, and why? A reading serif, with a sans for the interface. Source Serif 4 for reading and headings, Inter for labels and captions: a good magazine's text with a quiet interface. (because brand.q1, brand.q2, content.q1)
- scenarios.q1 Where do people use it? Anywhere, on any device. Readers arrive on phones and laptops alike. (because people.q1)
- scenarios.q2 How long is one visit? One sitting. A guide is read in one sitting. (because content.q1)
- team.q1 Who maintains the system? A small team. A small editorial team.
- team.q2 How fast does it change? Rarely. The design changes rarely.
- typography.roles Which text roles does it need? Core and editorial display. A lead and a display role open articles. (because content.q1)
- typography.count How many steps does the type scale take? Fine steps, so pages can set their own rhythm. Long pages need a clear hierarchy of headings, with fine steps between them. (because content.q1)
- typography.definition How are sizes and line heights defined? A ratio, line heights in proportion. Line height is a ratio, so it grows with the text. (because tasks.q1, people.q2)
- typography.values How large is body text? Large. Large body text is easy on the eyes. (because outcomes.q1)
- typography.lands Where does type do the most work? Articles and long text. Type does its work in articles. (because content.q1)
- color.roles Which color roles does it need? Surface, text, action and status. Reading needs few color roles. (because human.q1)
- color.count How many emphasis levels do actions need? Three. Primary, secondary and a text link. (because tasks.q2)
- color.definition How is the palette defined? Neutrals and one brand ramp. Warm paper neutrals and one ink ramp. (because brand.q1)
- color.values How saturated is the palette? Balanced. A calm, balanced palette. (because brand.q1)
- color.lands Where does color carry meaning first? Links and actions. Color marks links inside the text. (because tasks.q1)
- spacing.roles Which spacing roles does it need? Gaps and insets. No dense tables, so no row role. (because content.q1)
- spacing.count How many densities exist? One. One calm density. (because content.q2)
- spacing.definition How are spacing steps defined? Big, even steps. Big, even steps suit long reading. (because outcomes.q1)
- spacing.values How dense is the layout? Spacious. Room around the text helps reading. (because outcomes.q1)
- spacing.lands Where does spacing matter most? Between paragraphs. Space is spent between paragraphs and sections. (because content.q1)
- shape.roles Which shape roles does it need? Controls, badges and containers. Pill badges differ from controls. (because brand.q1)
- shape.count How many corner sizes exist? Three. Control, badge and container corners differ. (because shape.roles)
- shape.definition How are corners set? Fixed for the product. One brand, one set of corners. (because business.q2)
- shape.values What should control corners say? Rounded. Rounded corners feel friendly. (because brand.q1)
- shape.lands Where does shape show most? Controls and cards. Corners show on buttons and article cards. (because content.q1)
- elevation.roles What rises above the page? Only what floats. Only menus and dialogs float. (because human.q1)
- elevation.count How many shadow levels exist? One. One shadow for floating things. (because elevation.roles)
- elevation.definition What separates groups on the page? Space. Space separates groups; lines would interrupt reading. (because outcomes.q1)
- elevation.values How soft are shadows? Soft. Soft shadows suit warm paper. (because brand.q1)
- elevation.lands Where does elevation show? Menus and dialogs. Menus and dialogs are the only layers. (because elevation.roles)
- motion.roles What is motion for? Feedback and guidance. Motion confirms actions and guides between pages. (because people.q1)
- motion.count How many speeds exist? Two. One speed for feedback, one for panels. (because motion.roles)
- motion.definition How is easing defined? Standard ease-out. A standard ease-out is calm. (because brand.q1)
- motion.values How fast does feedback feel? Moderate. Moderate speed feels calm. (because brand.q1)
- motion.lands Where does motion show? State changes and panels. State changes and opening panels move. (because motion.roles)
- iconography.roles What do icons do? Actions, status and navigation. Occasional readers need icons for save, share and navigation. (because people.q1)
- iconography.count How many icon sizes exist? One. One size next to text. (because iconography.values)
- iconography.definition What icon style and stroke? Outline. Outline icons stay quiet beside text, at a 1.5px stroke. (because human.q1)
- iconography.values How big are icons next to text? Match the text. Icons match the text size. (because human.q1)
- iconography.lands Where do icons work hardest? Navigation. Icons help most in navigation. (because people.q1)
- theming.roles What can a theme change? Mode only. One brand, so only the mode changes. (because business.q2)
- theming.count How many themes ship? Two. Light and dark. (because theming.values)
- theming.definition How are brands handled? One brand. One publication, one brand. (because business.q2)
- theming.values Which modes ship? Light and dark. Light and dark ship as standard; dark helps night reading. (because scenarios.q1)
- theming.lands What changes when the theme changes? Colors only. Only colors change. (because theming.roles)
- accessibility.roles Which states get their own visible value? Those and pressed. Pressed gets its own value for touch. (because accessibility.values)
- accessibility.count How many signals carry each meaning? Two: color and word. Status is rare; color and a word are enough. (because people.q2)
- accessibility.definition What contrast floor do we hold? AA. AA contrast, with large text helping further. (because people.q2)
- accessibility.values What is the smallest target? Touch size. Readers are often on phones. (because scenarios.q1)
- accessibility.lands Where are the floors hardest to hold? Long text. Long text needs steady contrast and line length. (because content.q1)
- naming.roles What gets a name? Tokens and component keys. Components get their own keys. (because team.q2)
- naming.count How many token tiers? Three. Primitives, semantics and component keys. (because team.q2)
- naming.definition How are decisions named? By role. Role names survive a redesign. (because team.q1)
- naming.values How are names written? Lowercase words in paths. Lowercase paths read the same everywhere. (because team.q1)
- naming.lands What do components read? Component keys. A component API keeps changes local. (because team.q2)
- voice.roles Which kinds of copy does it need? Labels, messages and articles. Articles are the product; the UI copy must match them. (because content.q1)
- voice.count How many tones does it use? One per moment. Warm by default, calmer for errors. (because human.q1)
- voice.definition How is the voice defined? Principles and examples. Editors work from principles and examples, not word lists. (because team.q1, content.q1)
- voice.values How does it sound? Conversational. Talk to one reader, like a good editor. (because people.q1, brand.q1)
- voice.lands Where do the words matter most? Articles and guides. Most words are in articles and guides. (because content.q1)
- components.roles Which component families does it need? Core, plus content and media. Readers need sections, navigation and little else. (because content.q1, tasks.q1)
- components.count How far does the inventory reach? Only what today's screens use. Actions are rare, so the components today's pages use cover them. (because tasks.q2, team.q1)
- components.definition How does a component earn its place? A use scenario needs it. A component joins only when reading needs it. (because scenarios.q2, tasks.q1)
- components.values When does a component get another look? Only when the meaning changes. Pages stay calm when a component changes only with its meaning. (because brand.q2, outcomes.q1)
- components.lands Where do components do the most work? Articles. Components sit inside and around articles. (because content.q1)

### Usage rules

- Page title (page-title): use type.title; not type.display (landing only); Display is kept for the landing moment; article titles stay calm.
- A number in a table (number-in-table): use type.body; not A mono font; Tables are rare and read row by row, so digits never need to line up in columns. A mono font would break the reading voice.
- Paragraph or help text (paragraph): use type.body, at most 65 characters a line; not type.caption; A large size and short lines make long text easy on the eyes.
- Field label or column header (field-label): use type.label; not type.caption; Caption is too faint for a label people must read.
- A selected row or item (selected-row): use color.surface.selected; not Bold text only; A tint shows the choice clearly on warm paper.
- An error message (error-message): use color.status.danger and a plain sentence; not Color alone; The sentence says what to fix; color only draws the eye.
- A link (link): use color.text.link, underlined; not Color without underline; Readers expect links to be underlined inside text.
- A status (status-label): use Badge pill with a word; not An icon alone; Status is rare, so readers never learn an icon for it. A word is clear the first time.
- Items that belong together (related-items): use space.gap.default; not space.gap.tight; Text needs air even inside a group.
- Between page sections (between-sections): use space.gap.section, no line; not A divider line; Space alone separates sections; lines add noise.
- Table row height (table-row): use size.row (comfortable); not A compact row; Rows are read, not scanned.
- Corners of buttons and inputs (control-corner): use radius.control (rounded); not Sharp corners; Rounded corners match the warm reading tone. Sharp corners feel technical next to long text.
- Shape of a status badge (status-shape): use radius.badge (pill); not A rectangle; Pills sit softly next to text.
- A card on the page (card): use A border, no shadow; not A strong shadow; Cards stay flat on the page; shadows are for floating things.
- A menu or dialog (menu-or-dialog): use elevation.overlay and a dimmed page; not No shadow; The dimmed page focuses the reader on the dialog.
- Hover and press feedback (hover-feedback): use motion.duration.feedback (moderate); not A fast flash; Moderate speed feels calm in a slow reading flow. A fast flash feels jumpy.
- Someone asked for less motion (reduced-motion): use Fades only; nothing moves; not Reduced motion; Nothing slides or zooms for people who asked for less motion. A short fade keeps the change visible to the reader.
- An icon with no label (icon-alone): use Not used: always add a word; not An icon button; Occasional visitors do not know icons.
- Someone switches to dark (dark-mode): use The dark semantic mode; not Inverting images; Only semantic colors change; the reading layout stays.
- Keyboard focus (keyboard-focus): use button/focus-ring at focus.ring.width; not Removing the outline; Keyboard users must always see where they are.
- The smallest clickable thing (smallest-target): use size.control.default (touch); not A compact control; Many readers are on phones.
- The action that completes the task (commit-action): use Button primary, one per section; not Two primaries side by side; One clear action per section. Two primaries make the reader choose before they have read.
- An alternative or cancel (alternative-action): use Button ghost as a text link; not A second boxed button; A link feels lighter and does not compete.
- Delete or remove (destructive-action): use Button secondary with the full verb, then confirm with Button danger; not Button primary; Naming the verb and confirming prevents a mistake.
- An action on one row or item (row-action): use Button ghost with a word; not An icon on its own; Occasional visitors need the word.
- A value with no token (missing-token): use The closest semantic token, then ask for a new one; not A raw value in the component; Raw values break dark mode and the next redesign.
- A button label (button-label): use A warm verb a reader would say; not "Submit" or "Click here"; Buttons are part of the reading voice. Example: "Subscribe"
- The words of an error (error-words): use Calm and helpful. Take the blame, offer the way forward.; not Blaming the reader; A calm error keeps the reader's trust. Example: "We could not save your email. Check it and try again."
- A success message (success-words): use Warm and brief, with what happens next; not A bare "Done"; A warm close invites the reader back. Example: "You're in. The next issue arrives on Friday."
- An empty state (empty-words): use An invitation, not a dead end; not "No items"; An empty list is a chance to show what the product offers. Example: "Nothing saved yet. Tap Save on any article to read it later."
- A confirmation question (confirm-words): use Gentle and clear about what changes; not Guilt or pressure; Readers come back when leaving felt respectful. Example: "Unsubscribe from the weekly letter? You can come back any time."
- A first visit (first-visit): use One sentence on what is here and why it is worth reading; not A sign-up wall; Occasional readers decide in seconds whether to stay. Example: "Practical guides, one a week. Start with the most read."
- No component in the inventory fits (missing-component): use plain text, a link or a heading; not a new component for one article; Readers come for the words; extra parts pull the eye away from them.
- Hero line or key number (hero-line): use type.display; not type.display on article titles; On the landing hero only. One big serif line opens the publication. Articles keep calm titles, so the text gets the attention.
- Section heading (section-heading): use type.heading; not Bold body text; Clear headings let readers skim a long guide and find their place again.
- Supporting text (supporting-text): use type.caption; not type.body; Captions use the quiet interface face. Dates and notes never compete with the article.
- Text in a table cell (table-cell): use type.data; not A mono font; It equals body here. Tables are rare and read row by row. Cells use the reading face, so a row reads like a sentence.
- Title of a form page (form-page-title): use type.title; not type.display; Subscribe and account pages share the calm article title. The brand shows in the serif, not in size.
- Parts of one item (parts-of-one-item): use space.gap.tight; not space.gap.default; An icon and its word sit close. Readers who visit now and then see one item, not two.
- Items in a list or a form row (siblings-in-a-row): use space.gap.default; not space.gap.tight; Items in a list need air, so each one reads on its own.
- Between groups (between-groups): use space.gap.group; not space.gap.default; A clear step between groups gives the reader a place to pause.
- Inside a button or input (inside-a-control): use space.inset.control-x; not Padding set by eye; Wide padding gives each rare action room, so a button feels as calm as the text.
- Inside a card, panel or dialog (inside-a-container): use space.inset.container; not Text that touches the card edge; Generous padding frames each card like a page in a magazine.
- Inside a table cell (inside-a-cell): use space.inset.cell-x; not Narrow cell padding; Rows are read, not scanned. Cells get room like text does.
- An option in a menu or list (option-in-list): use radius.option; not radius.control; The option corner nests inside the menu corner. Soft, even curves keep the warm tone.
- Something that grows past one line (growing-element): use radius.element; not radius.surface; Text areas and list items share the control corner, so a form reads as one family.
- Corners of cards, menus and dialogs (surface-corner): use radius.surface; not radius.control; Softer corners on cards and menus feel warm, like good paper.
- Edges and dividers (edges-and-dividers): use border-width.default; not A heavy rule; A thin edge stays quiet beside long text. The words carry the page, not the lines.
- The gap around a focus ring (focus-gap): use focus.ring.offset; not A ring that touches the control; The ring stands clear of the control, so readers see focus on any fill.
- A panel opens (panel-opens): use motion.duration.panels; not An instant pop; A relaxed open guides the reader to the new panel without a jolt.
- The curve of any move (any-transition): use motion.easing.standard; not A bounce; A calm ease-out settles softly and never pulls the eye from the text.
- A hero or launch moment (hero-motion): use No hero motion: the landing stays still; not An animated headline; Attention belongs to the text. A moving headline pulls the eye away from it.
- An icon beside text (icon-beside-text): use size.icon and icon.stroke-width; not A filled or colored icon; Quiet outline icons sit beside the words and never outshine the text.
- Most buttons and inputs (most-controls): use size.control.default; not size.control.compact; Readers on phones get a full touch target on every control.
- The main action on a screen (main-action): use size.control.large; not A taller button for the main action; It is the same height as the default here. Actions are rare and calm. Color marks the main one; a bigger button would shout over the text.
- A button inside a field (control-inside-field): use size.control.compact; not size.control.default; A clear or show button must fit inside the field around it.
- A control that is not available yet (unavailable-control): use color.disabled.*, never opacity; not Hiding the control; Muted colors keep the control in place and its label readable. Hiding it would move the page and lose the reader's place.

### Voice and tone

Conversational and warm. Talk to one reader, like a good editor would. (follows voice.values, voice.roles)
- Write to one person: "you", not "users". (follows voice.values)
- Short sentences with room to breathe. (follows outcomes.q1)
- Explain why before asking for anything. (follows people.q1, voice.definition)
- A button label stays on one line: it never breaks onto two. (follows voice.values, voice.definition)
Use: Read, Save for later, You, Next issue. Avoid: Click here, Submit, Users, Content.
The tone per moment is in the usage rules of the voice situations above.

### Use scenarios

- A reader arrives from search on a phone and reads a long guide in one sitting. (follows scenarios.q1, scenarios.q2, people.q1)
- A returning reader saves an article to finish on the train. (follows scenarios.q1, content.q1)

## Dense data (dense-data)
