Dense data is an Open DS scheme: a full set of answers to the Open DS grammar, with the reasons behind each, usage rules, voice and tone, and the tokens that follow. Compact, exact and quiet, for analysts who scan alerts and compare signals all day.

Use when: Security operations, threat detection, model monitoring, admin panels and analytics: many records, daily expert users, mouse and keyboard.
Avoid when: Public sites, reading products, or first-time visitors on phones.
Themes: light, dark

### Answers

- business.q1 What does the product do for the business? Runs daily operations. The product runs daily security operations: alerts, incidents and the assets they touch.
- business.q2 How many brands or products share the system? One. One internal product, one brand.
- people.q1 Who uses it most? Daily experts. The same people use it all day, every day. (because business.q1)
- people.q2 What accessibility level do we commit to? AA. AA is the floor for an internal tool used by trained staff. (because people.q1)
- content.q1 What is the main content? Numbers and records. Most of the screen is numbers and records. (because business.q1)
- content.q2 How much is on one screen? A lot. Experts want many records on one screen. (because people.q1, content.q1)
- tasks.q1 What is the main task? Scan and compare. People scan rows and compare values. (because content.q1)
- tasks.q2 How often do people repeat actions? Constantly. The same actions repeat many times an hour. (because people.q1)
- human.q1 What must the interface protect? People keep their place. Losing your place in a long table costs time and errors. (because tasks.q1)
- human.q2 How do people recall the interface? They learn it and recognize it. Daily users learn the interface and recognize it. (because people.q1)
- outcomes.q1 Which outcome matters most? Time on task. Speed on repeated tasks is the measure. (because tasks.q2)
- outcomes.q2 What is a costly mistake? Acting on the wrong record. Acting on the wrong row is the costly error. (because tasks.q1)
- brand.q1 What should the brand feel like? Precise. The interface must feel exact and trustworthy. (because content.q1)
- brand.q2 How visible is the brand in the interface? Quiet. The data is the hero; the brand steps back. (because content.q2)
- brand.q3 Which typefaces carry the product, and why? A neutral grotesque, with a monospace for data. IBM Plex Sans for every text role and IBM Plex Mono for data: exact and quiet, so the numbers stay the hero. (because brand.q1, brand.q2, content.q1)
- scenarios.q1 Where do people use it? At a desk. Experts work at a desk with a mouse and keyboard. (because people.q1)
- scenarios.q2 How long is one visit? All day. The tool stays open for the whole shift. (because tasks.q2)
- team.q1 Who maintains the system? A small team. A small team keeps the system right.
- team.q2 How fast does it change? Every month. Features ship every month; the system must keep up.
- typography.roles Which text roles does it need? Core and data. A data role keeps numbers in aligned columns. (because content.q1, tasks.q1)
- typography.count How many steps does the type scale take? Only the steps the screens need. A screen full of records stays calm with only the sizes it needs. (because content.q2)
- typography.definition How are sizes and line heights defined? A ratio, line heights in proportion. Line height is a ratio of each text's own size, so it follows the text. Two steps: tight for headings and labels, open for body, data and captions. (because tasks.q1, people.q2)
- typography.values How large is body text? Small. Small body text fits more rows on the screen. (because content.q2)
- typography.lands Where does type do the most work? Tables and inputs. Most text sits in table cells and inputs. (because content.q1)
- color.roles Which color roles does it need? Surface, text, action and status. Surface, text, action and status cover an operations tool. (because brand.q2)
- color.count How many emphasis levels do actions need? Three. One primary per view; the rest step back. (because tasks.q2)
- color.definition How is the palette defined? Neutrals and one brand ramp. One product, one brand ramp on cool neutrals. (because business.q2)
- color.values How saturated is the palette? Muted. Muted color keeps attention on the data. (because brand.q2)
- color.lands Where does color carry meaning first? Status in tables. Color earns its place by marking late and failed records. (because outcomes.q2)
- spacing.roles Which spacing roles does it need? Gaps, insets and row heights. Row height is a decision of its own in a table product. (because content.q1)
- spacing.count How many densities exist? Two. A second, denser size serves tables and toolbars. (because tasks.q1)
- spacing.definition How are spacing steps defined? Small steps, on a 4px grid. Steps on a 4px grid give the small gaps dense screens need. (because content.q2)
- spacing.values How dense is the layout? Compact. Compact spacing shows more records. (because content.q2)
- spacing.lands Where does spacing matter most? Rows and cells. Space is spent inside rows and cells. (because tasks.q1)
- shape.roles Which shape roles does it need? Controls, badges and containers. Badges sit in columns and need their own corner. (because tasks.q1)
- shape.count How many corner sizes exist? Three. Control, badge and container corners differ. (because shape.roles)
- shape.definition How are corners set? Fixed for the product. One brand, one fixed set of corners. (because business.q2)
- shape.values What should control corners say? Slightly rounded. Small corners keep dense rows straight. (because brand.q1)
- shape.lands Where does shape show most? Controls in dense rows. Corners show most on controls in dense rows. (because content.q2)
- elevation.roles What rises above the page? Only what floats. Only menus and dialogs float; cards use lines. (because elevation.definition)
- elevation.count How many shadow levels exist? One. One shadow for everything that floats. (because elevation.roles)
- elevation.definition What separates groups on the page? Lines. Thin lines guide the eye along rows. (because human.q1)
- elevation.values How soft are shadows? Subtle. Subtle shadows keep the grid crisp. (because brand.q1)
- elevation.lands Where does elevation show? Menus and dialogs. Menus and dialogs are the only layers. (because elevation.roles)
- motion.roles What is motion for? Feedback only. Motion confirms an action; nothing else moves. (because human.q1)
- motion.count How many speeds exist? One. One speed is enough for feedback. (because motion.roles)
- motion.definition How is easing defined? Standard ease-out. A standard ease-out never draws attention. (because brand.q1)
- motion.values How fast does feedback feel? Fast. Fast feedback keeps up with experts. (because outcomes.q1)
- motion.lands Where does motion show? State changes only. Only state changes move. (because motion.roles)
- iconography.roles What do icons do? Actions and status. Icons mark row actions and status. (because tasks.q2)
- iconography.count How many icon sizes exist? One. One size, matched to the small text. (because typography.values)
- iconography.definition What icon style and stroke? Outline. Outline icons at a 1.5px stroke stay light next to dense text. (because content.q2)
- iconography.values How big are icons next to text? Match the text. Icons match the label so they do not outweigh it. (because content.q2)
- iconography.lands Where do icons work hardest? Toolbars and rows. Icons work hardest in toolbars and row actions. (because tasks.q2)
- theming.roles What can a theme change? Mode only. One brand, so only the mode changes. (because business.q2)
- theming.count How many themes ship? Two. Light and dark. (because theming.values)
- theming.definition How are brands handled? One brand. One product, one brand. (because business.q2)
- theming.values Which modes ship? Light and dark. Light first, always; dark ships as standard for night shifts. (because scenarios.q2)
- theming.lands What changes when the theme changes? Colors only. A mode switch changes colors only, so layout never moves. (because human.q1)
- accessibility.roles Which states get their own visible value? Hover, focus, disabled. Pressed reuses hover; experts do not need more. (because people.q1)
- accessibility.count How many signals carry each meaning? Three: color, icon and word. Many statuses share one table; color alone is not enough. (because people.q2, content.q1)
- accessibility.definition What contrast floor do we hold? AA. AA contrast for every text. (because people.q2)
- accessibility.values What is the smallest target? Compact, for a pointer. Mouse and keyboard; compact targets are enough. (because scenarios.q1)
- accessibility.lands Where are the floors hardest to hold? Dense tables. Small text and thin lines in tables need the most care. (because content.q2)
- naming.roles What gets a name? Tokens and component keys. Components get their own keys. (because team.q2)
- naming.count How many token tiers? Three. Primitives, semantics and component keys. (because team.q2)
- naming.definition How are decisions named? By role. Role names survive a redesign. (because team.q1)
- naming.values How are names written? Lowercase words in paths. Lowercase paths read the same in CSS, JSON and Figma. (because team.q1)
- naming.lands What do components read? Component keys. A component API keeps changes local. (because team.q2)
- voice.roles Which kinds of copy does it need? Labels and messages. Labels and messages are all the copy an operations tool needs. (because business.q1)
- voice.count How many tones does it use? One. One flat tone everywhere; experts want no surprises. (because people.q1)
- voice.definition How is the voice defined? Rules and a word list. A word list keeps labels identical across screens. (because team.q1, tasks.q2)
- voice.values How does it sound? Terse. Experts want short labels and short messages. (because people.q1, brand.q1)
- voice.lands Where do the words matter most? Errors and empty states. Errors and empty tables are where words decide the next action. (because outcomes.q2)
- components.roles Which component families does it need? Core, plus data. Records need tables, filters and fast ways to move between them. (because content.q1, tasks.q1)
- components.count How far does the inventory reach? What today's screens use, plus what the next ones will likely need. A full operations tool with the parts its next screens will need, still few enough for a small team to keep right. (because content.q2, team.q1)
- components.definition How does a component earn its place? A use scenario needs it. A component joins only when a daily task needs it. (because scenarios.q1, tasks.q2)
- components.values When does a component get another look? Only when the meaning changes. Repeated screens stay identical when a component changes only with its meaning. (because brand.q2, tasks.q2)
- components.lands Where do components do the most work? Tables and forms. Most work happens in tables and the forms that edit them. (because content.q1, tasks.q1)

### Usage rules

- Page title (page-title): use type.title; not type.display; Titles stay small so the table starts higher on the screen.
- A number in a table (number-in-table): use type.data; not type.body; Mono digits line up in columns, so values compare at a glance.
- Paragraph or help text (paragraph): use type.body; not type.label; Help text is a sentence read in passing. Body size reads quickly; the label style is made for short names, not sentences.
- Field label or column header (field-label): use type.label; not type.heading; Headers repeat on every column; a heavy style would compete with the data.
- A selected row or item (selected-row): use color.surface.selected; not color.action.primary as a fill; A light tint shows selection without hiding the data.
- An error message (error-message): use color.status.danger with an icon; not color.status.warning; Red always means fix this, and the icon says it without color.
- A link (link): use color.text.link; not color.action.primary; Links and buttons look different, so people know which one navigates.
- A status (status-label): use Badge with a subtle fill, an icon and a word; not A full-strength fill; Subtle fills let many statuses share one table.
- Items that belong together (related-items): use space.gap.tight; not space.gap.group; Things that belong together sit close.
- Between page sections (between-sections): use space.gap.section and a hairline; not A card around every section; Lines separate without taking room from the data.
- Table row height (table-row): use size.row (compact); not The comfortable row; Compact rows show more records without scrolling.
- Corners of buttons and inputs (control-corner): use radius.control; not radius.round; Small corners keep dense rows straight.
- Shape of a status badge (status-shape): use radius.badge (rectangle); not A pill; Rectangles line up in a column.
- A card on the page (card): use A hairline border, no shadow; not A shadow; On a busy grid, lines separate. Shadows blur the edges.
- A menu or dialog (menu-or-dialog): use elevation.overlay and a dimmed page for dialogs; not A border only; Floating things need a shadow so they read as on top.
- Hover and press feedback (hover-feedback): use motion.duration.feedback (fast); not No transition; Fast feedback confirms the pointer without slowing experts.
- Someone asked for less motion (reduced-motion): use Fades only; nothing moves; not A shorter version of the motion; Movement stops when people ask for less motion. A short fade still confirms a change without moving anything.
- An icon with no label (icon-alone): use Icon button with a tooltip; not A bare icon; Experts learn icons; the tooltip covers the first uses.
- Someone switches to dark (dark-mode): use The dark semantic mode; not A second palette in components; Only semantic colors change, so layout never moves.
- Keyboard focus (keyboard-focus): use button/focus-ring at focus.ring.width; not Removing the outline; Keyboard users must always see where they are.
- The smallest clickable thing (smallest-target): use size.control.compact; not Anything smaller; Compact still fits a mouse. Touch is not this product's input.
- The action that completes the task (commit-action): use Button primary, one per view; not Two primaries side by side; One primary makes the committing action obvious.
- An alternative or cancel (alternative-action): use Button secondary; not Button ghost; A ghost button has no edge, so next to a filled primary it reads as plain text and cancel gets lost. Secondary keeps a visible border, so people find it at once.
- Delete or remove (destructive-action): use Button secondary, then confirm in a dialog with Button danger; not Button primary as the first step; Deleting is rare and costly; a confirm step catches mistakes.
- An action on one row or item (row-action): use Icon button, ghost, compact; not Button secondary in every row; Rows repeat dozens of times; a quiet icon keeps the table readable.
- A value with no token (missing-token): use The closest semantic token, then ask for a new one; not A raw value in the component; Raw values break dark mode and the next redesign.
- A button label (button-label): use One verb from the word list; not A sentence or "Please"; Labels repeat on every screen; one verb reads fastest. Example: "Export"
- The words of an error (error-words): use Name the record, then the fix. Flat and specific.; not "Oops" or a vague apology; Experts act on the message; the record and the fix are all they need. Example: "Alert ALR-2042 not saved. Threshold must be between 0 and 100."
- A success message (success-words): use A short confirmation with the count; not Celebration; Confirm and get out of the way; the next task is waiting. Example: "12 alerts exported."
- An empty state (empty-words): use Why it is empty and the one action that fills it; not A blank table; An empty table with no words looks like an error. Example: "No escalated alerts. Change the date range to see older ones."
- A confirmation question (confirm-words): use Name the exact object and the consequence; not "Are you sure?"; Acting on the wrong record is the costly mistake. Example: "Dismiss 3 alerts? This cannot be undone."
- A first visit (first-visit): use No tour. Show the data, with a tooltip where needed.; not A welcome tour; Daily experts skip tours; tooltips cover the first uses. Example: "Hover any column header to see what it counts."
- No component in the inventory fits (missing-component): use a component from the inventory, composed (for example a popover with a command list); not a one-off component built for one screen; A small team keeps fewer parts right, and experts expect the same parts everywhere.
- Hero line or key number (hero-line): use type.display; not type.display for page titles; It is for the one key number at the top of a dashboard. One big total gives analysts the headline at a glance. Everything below it stays small so more rows fit.
- Section heading (section-heading): use type.heading; not type.title; Panel and card headings sit one step above body. They name a block without taking rows from the data.
- Supporting text (supporting-text): use type.caption; not type.body; Timestamps and hints step back, so the values stay the hero.
- Text in a table cell (table-cell): use type.data; not type.body; Every cell shares the mono face, so IDs, times and values line up down each column.
- Title of a form page (form-page-title): use type.title; not type.display; Settings and form pages keep the same small title as every page. Experts find the fields higher up.
- Parts of one item (parts-of-one-item): use space.gap.tight; not space.gap.default; An icon and its word sit close, so each item reads as one unit in a dense row.
- Items in a list or a form row (siblings-in-a-row): use space.gap.default; not space.gap.tight; Items in a list sit close but apart. Analysts still tell one record from the next.
- Between groups (between-groups): use space.gap.group; not space.gap.section; A small step marks a new group without pushing records off the screen.
- Inside a button or input (inside-a-control): use space.inset.control-x; not Padding set by eye; Narrow padding keeps buttons short, so a toolbar holds every action an expert repeats.
- Inside a card, panel or dialog (inside-a-container): use space.inset.container; not space.gap.section; Cards and dialogs keep a small inset, so their content starts close to the edge.
- Inside a table cell (inside-a-cell): use space.inset.cell-x; not space.inset.container; Narrow cell padding fits more columns, and values in two columns still stay apart.
- An option in a menu or list (option-in-list): use radius.option; not radius.control; Options sit square inside the menu. A long list scans as one clean column.
- Something that grows past one line (growing-element): use radius.element; not radius.surface; Rows and text areas keep the small control corner, so long lists stay straight.
- Corners of cards, menus and dialogs (surface-corner): use radius.surface; not radius.control; Cards and menus get a corner just softer than controls. Panels still tile neatly on a busy screen.
- Edges and dividers (edges-and-dividers): use border-width.default; not A thicker border; A hairline separates rows and cards without taking room from the data.
- The gap around a focus ring (focus-gap): use focus.ring.offset; not A ring that touches the control; The gap keeps the ring clear of the control. Keyboard users see which row has focus and act on the right one.
- A panel opens (panel-opens): use motion.duration.panels; not A slow slide-in; Panels open at the feedback speed, so experts never wait for a menu.
- The curve of any move (any-transition): use motion.easing.standard; not A spring or a bounce; A plain ease-out starts fast and settles quietly. Nothing pulls the eye from the data.
- A hero or launch moment (hero-motion): use No hero motion; not An intro animation; Analysts open the tool to work for a whole shift. An intro would cost time on every visit.
- An icon beside text (icon-beside-text): use size.icon and icon.stroke-width; not An icon larger than its label; Icons match the small text, so a toolbar reads as one line. The light stroke keeps rows quiet.
- Most buttons and inputs (most-controls): use size.control.default; not size.control.large; Buttons and inputs fit a mouse and keep toolbars short.
- The main action on a screen (main-action): use size.control.large; not A taller button for the main action; It is the same height as the default here. Color and place mark the main action. One height keeps toolbar buttons in line.
- A button inside a field (control-inside-field): use size.control.compact; not size.control.default; A clear or step button fits inside the field, so the field keeps its row height.
- A control that is not available yet (unavailable-control): use color.disabled.*, never opacity; not Hiding the control; Muted colors keep a disabled control in its place and its label readable. Experts keep their bearings and see the action will come back.

### Voice and tone

Terse and exact. Say what happened and what to do, in as few words as possible. (follows voice.values, people.q1)
- Lead with the object, then the state: "Alert 2041 contained." (follows voice.values, content.q1)
- Use numbers, not words for numbers. (follows content.q1)
- One verb per button. No "please", no exclamation marks. (follows voice.definition, voice.values)
- A button label stays on one line: it never breaks onto two. (follows voice.values, voice.definition)
Use: Investigate, Filter, Assign, Escalated, Resolved. Avoid: Oops, Awesome, Please, Simply.
The tone per moment is in the usage rules of the voice situations above.

### Use scenarios

- A security analyst opens the alert queue at 8:00 and scans 200 rows for escalated threats. (follows scenarios.q1, scenarios.q2, tasks.q1)
- An analyst compares this week's detections with last week's, model by model and column by column. (follows tasks.q1, content.q1)

## Multi-brand (multi-brand)

Multi-brand is an Open DS scheme: a full set of answers to the Open DS grammar, with the reasons behind each, usage rules, voice and tone, and the tokens that follow. Customer screens for several brands, often on phones: sign-up, checkout, account. Components never change; brand primitives do.

Use when: Companies that sell to customers under several brands, or white-label products shown to their clients' customers: sign-up, checkout, account and product pages.
Avoid when: A single product with one brand, where the brand layer is cost with no user; or tools staff use all day. Use Dense data for those.
Themes: aster-light, aster-dark, birch-light, birch-dark, coral-light, coral-dark

### Answers

- business.q1 What does the product do for the business? Sells and converts. A company sells several products under several brands.
- business.q2 How many brands or products share the system? Many. Three brands share one system today, more tomorrow. (because business.q1)
- people.q1 Who uses it most? Customers who choose us. Customers who chose one of our brands. (because business.q1)
- people.q2 What accessibility level do we commit to? AA. AA in every brand. (because people.q1)
- content.q1 What is the main content? Forms and tasks. Product pages, sign-up and account forms. (because business.q1)
- content.q2 How much is on one screen? A moderate amount. A moderate amount per screen. (because content.q1)
- tasks.q1 What is the main task? Complete a form. Customers sign up and buy. (because business.q1)
- tasks.q2 How often do people repeat actions? Sometimes. Customers return now and then. (because people.q1)
- human.q1 What must the interface protect? Low effort to understand. Low effort, whichever brand they see. (because people.q1)
- human.q2 How do people recall the interface? They see it fresh each time. Customers see it fresh each time. (because tasks.q2)
- outcomes.q1 Which outcome matters most? Completion without errors. Finished sign-ups and orders. (because tasks.q1)
- outcomes.q2 What is a costly mistake? Looking off-brand. A page that looks like the wrong brand loses trust. (because business.q2)
- brand.q1 What should the brand feel like? Neutral and adaptable. A neutral base each brand can color. (because business.q2)
- brand.q2 How visible is the brand in the interface? Present. Each brand is clearly present. (because business.q2)
- brand.q3 Which typefaces carry the product, and why? Each brand brings its own face, on one shared scale. Each brand brings its own face, Inter, Plus Jakarta Sans or Poppins, on one shared type scale, so brands differ and the system stays one. (because business.q2, brand.q1, brand.q2)
- scenarios.q1 Where do people use it? Anywhere, on any device. Customers sign up on phones and manage plans on laptops. (because people.q1)
- scenarios.q2 How long is one visit? A few minutes. Most visits are a few minutes: sign up, check, change. (because tasks.q1)
- team.q1 Who maintains the system? A platform team. A platform team serves three product teams. (because business.q2)
- team.q2 How fast does it change? Every month. Brands ship every month. (because business.q2)
- typography.roles Which text roles does it need? Core: heading, body, label. One set of roles across brands. (because business.q2)
- typography.count How many steps does the type scale take? One step per kind of text. One size per kind of text suits every brand font. (because business.q2)
- typography.definition How are sizes and line heights defined? A ratio, line heights in proportion. Ratios work with every brand font. (because business.q2)
- typography.values How large is body text? Regular. Regular body size suits all brands. (because brand.q1)
- typography.lands Where does type do the most work? Forms and labels. Sign-up and account forms carry most text. (because tasks.q1)
- color.roles Which color roles does it need? Those and brand accents. Each brand brings its own accent ramp. (because business.q2)
- color.count How many emphasis levels do actions need? Three. Primary, secondary and ghost in every brand. (because tasks.q1)
- color.definition How is the palette defined? Shared neutrals, a ramp per brand. Shared neutrals; each brand sets its own ramp. (because business.q2)
- color.values How saturated is the palette? Balanced. Balanced, so any brand hue works. (because brand.q1)
- color.lands Where does color carry meaning first? Brand moments. Brand color shows on actions and headlines. (because brand.q2)
- spacing.roles Which spacing roles does it need? Gaps, insets and row heights. Account tables need a row height. (because content.q1)
- spacing.count How many densities exist? One. One density across brands. (because business.q2)
- spacing.definition How are spacing steps defined? Small steps, on a 4px grid. Every brand shares one set of steps, so they sit on a 4px grid: small enough for account forms, with big ones for product pages. (because business.q2)
- spacing.values How dense is the layout? Comfortable. Comfortable spacing in every brand. (because content.q2)
- spacing.lands Where does spacing matter most? Between fields. Space matters most between form fields. (because tasks.q1)
- shape.roles Which shape roles does it need? Controls, badges and containers. Each brand sets three corners. (because business.q2)
- shape.count How many corner sizes exist? Two. Two corner sizes: one for controls and badges, and a larger one for containers, as Aster's 4px and 8px corners show. (because shape.roles, shape.values)
- shape.definition How are corners set? Set by each brand. Each brand sets its own corners. (because business.q2)
- shape.values What should control corners say? Rounded. Rounded by default; each brand sets its own corner. (because business.q2)
- shape.lands Where does shape show most? Buttons and badges. Corners are the most visible brand difference. (because brand.q2)
- elevation.roles What rises above the page? Cards too. Cards lift slightly to group offers. (because elevation.definition)
- elevation.count How many shadow levels exist? Two. One shadow for cards, one for overlays. (because elevation.roles)
- elevation.definition What separates groups on the page? Cards. Cards group plans and offers. (because content.q1)
- elevation.values How soft are shadows? Soft. Soft shadows fit every brand. (because brand.q1)
- elevation.lands Where does elevation show? Cards, menus and dialogs. Cards, menus and dialogs rise. (because elevation.roles)
- motion.roles What is motion for? Feedback and guidance. Feedback and guidance through sign-up. (because tasks.q1)
- motion.count How many speeds exist? Two. One speed for feedback, one for panels. (because motion.roles)
- motion.definition How is easing defined? Standard ease-out. A standard ease-out across brands. (because business.q2)
- motion.values How fast does feedback feel? Moderate. Moderate speed across brands. (because brand.q1)
- motion.lands Where does motion show? State changes and panels. State changes and panels move. (because motion.roles)
- iconography.roles What do icons do? Actions, status and navigation. Icons for actions, status and navigation. (because people.q1)
- iconography.count How many icon sizes exist? One. One size next to text. (because iconography.values)
- iconography.definition What icon style and stroke? Outline. One outline set for every brand, at a 1.5px stroke. (because business.q2)
- iconography.values How big are icons next to text? Match the text. Icons match the text. (because business.q2)
- iconography.lands Where do icons work hardest? Navigation. Icons help most in navigation. (because people.q1)
- theming.roles What can a theme change? Mode and brand. Brand and mode both change. (because business.q2)
- theming.count How many themes ship? Several. Three brands in light and dark: six themes. (because business.q2, theming.values)
- theming.definition How are brands handled? Brands as modes. Brands are theme modes over shared semantics. (because business.q2)
- theming.values Which modes ship? Light and dark. Light and dark ship for every brand. (because business.q2)
- theming.lands What changes when the theme changes? Colors, type and shape. A brand switch changes colors, fonts and corners. (because theming.roles)
- accessibility.roles Which states get their own visible value? Those and pressed. Pressed for touch. (because accessibility.values)
- accessibility.count How many signals carry each meaning? Two: color and word. Brand colors vary, so meaning needs a word. (because business.q2)
- accessibility.definition What contrast floor do we hold? AA. AA in every brand and mode. (because people.q2)
- accessibility.values What is the smallest target? Touch size. Customers sign up on phones. (because scenarios.q1)
- accessibility.lands Where are the floors hardest to hold? Brand color. Brand colors must pass in every mode. (because business.q2)
- naming.roles What gets a name? Tokens and component keys. Components get their own keys, shared by every brand. (because business.q2)
- naming.count How many token tiers? Three. Primitives, semantics and component keys. (because team.q2)
- naming.definition How are decisions named? By role. Role names stay the same in every brand. (because business.q2)
- naming.values How are names written? Lowercase words in paths. Lowercase paths read the same everywhere. (because team.q1)
- naming.lands What do components read? Component keys. Components never change; brand primitives do. (because business.q2)
- voice.roles Which kinds of copy does it need? Labels, messages and headlines. Each brand has headlines on top of shared UI copy. (because business.q2)
- voice.count How many tones does it use? One per brand. A shared core, with a tone per brand. (because business.q2)
- voice.definition How is the voice defined? A shared core, brand tone on top. Errors and confirmations are shared; brand tone sits on top. (because business.q2, team.q1)
- voice.values How does it sound? Plain and direct. The shared core is plain and direct. (because brand.q1)
- voice.lands Where do the words matter most? Headlines and buttons. Brand tone shows in headlines and buttons. (because brand.q2)
- components.roles Which component families does it need? Core, plus content and media. Product teams build sign-up and account forms, plus product pages with questions and faces. (because content.q1, team.q1)
- components.count How far does the inventory reach? What today's screens use, plus what the next ones will likely need. Three product teams find their next parts ready, kept by one platform team. (because team.q1, team.q2)
- components.definition How does a component earn its place? Its family is in the roles, so product teams find it ready. Product teams find a whole family ready instead of asking one by one. (because team.q1, team.q2)
- components.values When does a component get another look? Also for emphasis and size. Variants for emphasis and size let each brand feel present without new components. (because brand.q2, outcomes.q2)
- components.lands Where do components do the most work? Sign-up and account pages. Most components sit in sign-up and account pages. (because content.q1, tasks.q1)

### Usage rules

- Page title (page-title): use type.title in the brand font; not A brand-specific style; Roles stay shared; only the brand font changes.
- A number in a table (number-in-table): use type.body; not A mono font; Prices sit in sentences and offers, not in columns to compare, so a mono font adds nothing in any brand.
- Paragraph or help text (paragraph): use type.body; not type.caption; Regular body size suits every brand.
- Field label or column header (field-label): use type.label; not type.caption; Labels stay readable in every brand.
- A selected row or item (selected-row): use color.surface.selected (from the brand); not A fixed blue; Selection follows the brand color.
- An error message (error-message): use color.status.danger and a sentence; not The brand color; Status colors are shared, never branded.
- A link (link): use color.text.link (from the brand); not A fixed blue; Links take the brand's color, so they look native in each brand. A fixed blue would clash with some brands.
- A status (status-label): use Badge with a word; not A brand color as status; Brand hues vary, so meaning needs a word.
- Items that belong together (related-items): use space.gap.default; not Brand-specific spacing; Spacing is shared across brands.
- Between page sections (between-sections): use space.gap.section and cards; not Lines; Cards hold each offer together, so customers compare offers as units in every brand. Lines would split an offer apart.
- Table row height (table-row): use size.row (comfortable); not A compact row; Customers browse on phones, and compact rows are hard to tap in any brand.
- Corners of buttons and inputs (control-corner): use radius.control (set by the brand); not A hard-coded radius; Each brand sets its own corner through the theme.
- Shape of a status badge (status-shape): use radius.badge (set by the brand); not A hard-coded shape; The brand sets the badge shape.
- A card on the page (card): use elevation.card; none in dark; not A border only; Cards lift slightly to group offers. In dark, tone and a ring do the lift, the same in every brand.
- A menu or dialog (menu-or-dialog): use elevation.overlay and a dimmed page; not No shadow; The shadow shows a menu or dialog floats above the page. Without it, it blends into the cards.
- Hover and press feedback (hover-feedback): use motion.duration.feedback (moderate); not Brand-specific motion; Motion is shared, so one component library behaves the same in every brand.
- Someone asked for less motion (reduced-motion): use Fades only; nothing moves; not Full motion; Motion is reduced, not removed: a fade keeps the change visible, and nothing slides.
- An icon with no label (icon-alone): use Not used: always add a word; a popover explains a fee; not An icon button with a hover hint; On touch screens hover hints never show; a word says what will happen.
- Someone switches to dark (dark-mode): use The dark mode of the active brand; not One dark theme for all brands; Every brand ships light and dark.
- Keyboard focus (keyboard-focus): use button/focus-ring (from the brand) at focus.ring.width; not Removing the outline; Focus follows the brand but always shows.
- The smallest clickable thing (smallest-target): use size.control.default (touch); not A compact control; Customers are often on phones.
- The action that completes the task (commit-action): use Button primary, one per view; not Two primaries; One clear action per view. Two primaries split attention.
- An alternative or cancel (alternative-action): use Button secondary; not A second primary; The alternative steps back, so the one primary stays clear. A second primary would compete with it.
- Delete or remove (destructive-action): use Button secondary, then confirm with Button danger; not Button primary; Confirm before destroying data.
- An action on one row or item (row-action): use Button ghost with a word; not An icon alone; A word says what will happen.
- A value with no token (missing-token): use The closest semantic token, then ask for a new one; not A raw value or a brand primitive in the component; A raw value shows the same in every brand, so it breaks the theme.
- A button label (button-label): use A shared verb; the brand may choose the headline verb; not Brand slang on account actions; Shared labels keep the account area the same in every brand. Example: "Get started"
- The words of an error (error-words): use Shared across brands: plain and specific; not Brand tone in errors; Errors read the same in every brand, so support can help anyone. Example: "Your card was declined. Try another card or contact your bank."
- A success message (success-words): use Brand tone allowed: Aster calm, Birch friendly, Coral upbeat; not The same flat line in every brand; Success is a safe moment for brand tone. Example: "Aster: Your plan is active. · Birch: You're all set! · Coral: Let's go, your plan is live."
- An empty state (empty-words): use Shared structure, brand words; not A different structure per brand; The structure is the shared core; words carry the brand. Example: "No orders yet. Your first order will appear here."
- A confirmation question (confirm-words): use Shared across brands: plain and specific; not Brand tone when something is lost; Loss is never the moment for personality. Example: "Cancel your plan? It stays active until the end of the month."
- A first visit (first-visit): use Brand tone in the first headline only; not Brand tone in every line; One headline carries the brand; the rest stays shared. Example: "Birch: Hi! Let's set up your plan."
- No component in the inventory fits (missing-component): use a component from the inventory with brand tokens; not a component made for one brand; Brands change primitives, never components; one brand-only part breaks the shared library.
- Hero line or key number (hero-line): use type.display; not A brand-specific headline style; In the brand font for the product-page headline. Each brand speaks loudest in its product headline, on the shared scale.
- Section heading (section-heading): use type.heading; not Bold body text; Headings stay one shared role; only the brand font changes.
- Supporting text (supporting-text): use type.caption; not A brand-specific small style; One caption role serves fees, dates and hints in every brand.
- Text in a table cell (table-cell): use type.data; not A mono font; It equals body here. Plan and order tables read like body text in every brand font.
- Title of a form page (form-page-title): use type.title; not type.display; In the brand font. Sign-up and account pages share one title role in every brand.
- Parts of one item (parts-of-one-item): use space.gap.tight; not Brand-specific spacing; Parts of one item sit close in every brand, so the shared parts look the same.
- Items in a list or a form row (siblings-in-a-row): use space.gap.default; not space.gap.tight; Fields in a form keep a comfortable gap, so customers on phones tap the right one.
- Between groups (between-groups): use space.gap.group; not Brand-specific spacing; One group gap in every brand keeps sign-up forms the same shape.
- Inside a button or input (inside-a-control): use space.inset.control-x; not Brand-specific padding; Shared padding keeps buttons the same size in every brand.
- Inside a card, panel or dialog (inside-a-container): use space.inset.container; not Brand-specific padding; Cards hold offers the same way in every brand; only the corner and color change.
- Inside a table cell (inside-a-cell): use space.inset.cell-x; not Narrow cell padding; Account tables keep room between columns on a phone in every brand.
- An option in a menu or list (option-in-list): use radius.option; not A hard-coded radius; (set by the brand). Each brand sets the option corner, and it nests inside that brand's menu corner.
- Something that grows past one line (growing-element): use radius.element; not radius.control; (set by the brand). A brand with pill controls would turn a text area into a capsule. The element corner stays sane in every brand.
- Corners of cards, menus and dialogs (surface-corner): use radius.surface; not A hard-coded radius; (set by the brand). Each brand sets its own card corner; the role stays shared.
- Edges and dividers (edges-and-dividers): use border-width.default; not A brand-specific border width; One thin edge serves every brand. Color carries the brand, not line weight.
- The gap around a focus ring (focus-gap): use focus.ring.offset; not A ring that touches the control; The gap sits around a ring of focus.ring.width. The ring and its gap stay the same in every brand, so focus shows on any brand color.
- A panel opens (panel-opens): use motion.duration.panels; not Brand-specific motion; A relaxed open guides customers through sign-up the same way in every brand.
- The curve of any move (any-transition): use motion.easing.standard; not A brand-specific curve; One calm curve keeps the shared components the same in every brand.
- A hero or launch moment (hero-motion): use No hero motion; not An intro animation for one brand; A brand-only animation would break the shared library.
- An icon beside text (icon-beside-text): use size.icon and icon.stroke-width; not A brand-specific icon set; One icon set and size serve every brand; only the color changes.
- Most buttons and inputs (most-controls): use size.control.default; not size.control.compact; Customers sign up on phones, so every control fits a thumb in every brand.
- The main action on a screen (main-action): use size.control.large; not A taller button for one brand; It is the same height as the default here. Brand color marks the main action. One height keeps every brand's forms the same.
- A button inside a field (control-inside-field): use size.control.compact; not size.control.default; A clear or show-password button fits inside the field in every brand.
- A control that is not available yet (unavailable-control): use color.disabled.*, never opacity; not A grey color per brand; One set of muted colors works under every brand, and the label stays readable where a fade would lose it.

### Voice and tone

A plain shared voice. Each brand adds its own tone on top, never its own structure. (follows voice.definition, voice.count)
- Shared structure: object, state, next step. (follows voice.definition)
- Brand tone lives in headlines and marketing copy, not in errors. (follows voice.lands, voice.count)
- Errors and confirmations read the same in every brand. (follows voice.definition)
- A button label stays on one line: it never breaks onto two. (follows voice.values, voice.definition)
Use: Get started, Plan, Order. Avoid: Brand-specific words in errors, Jargon.
The tone per moment is in the usage rules of the voice situations above.

### Use scenarios

- A customer signs up for a plan on the Birch site, then manages it in the shared account area. (follows scenarios.q1, scenarios.q2, business.q2)
- A product team launches a fourth brand by adding brand primitives, without touching components. (follows business.q2, team.q2)
